=== CALL C0449 ===
Darren: Hello! Can you hear me alright? There we go. Gareth, is it?
Gareth: Yeah. Hi. I can hear you fine.
Darren: Lovely. I'm Darren. I've got to say, I clocked that scarf on your wall in the photo. Saints fan?
Gareth: Er, yeah. Since I was a kid. Season ticket, though I only make about half the games.
Darren: No way. Me too, well, not a season ticket, I'm more of a pub man, but I get down St Mary's a few times a season with a mate. Saturday though, eh? Rubbish.
Gareth: Yeah, that was poor. No shape in the second half at all.
Darren: None. I was sat in the Red Lion shouting at the telly like it was gonna help. Anyway, yeah. Where are you, then?
Gareth: Andover. Grew up in Basingstoke though.
Darren: Get out. I'm Basingstoke, born and bred, still here. Which school?
Gareth: Er, I went to the sixth-form college after. You'd probably know it.
Darren: Oh yeah, I know it. I didn't last that long, me, I was out at sixteen and on a trade counter. Builders' merchants. Been there over twenty years now, I'm branch manager, so it's timber, plumbing, heavy-side, all that, about fourteen staff. And you?
Gareth: Warehousing and distribution. Three sites along the M3 and the A303. I'm operations director.
Darren: Director, very nice. So you'll know the M3 roadworks, then.
Gareth: Every morning. I'm in early for the handover, so I miss the worst of it, but the way back's grim.
Darren: It's a nightmare, mate. I sat on it Tuesday for forty minutes. Got done by a speed camera on the A33 the week before, as well, so I'm not having much luck with roads at the minute. Company car, so I sort of tell myself it's not my petrol, you know, but the points are still mine.
Gareth: Yeah. That's the bit that matters.
Darren: Do you get a car with yours?
Gareth: Er, I do, yeah. They offered me an upgrade last year, but we had a pay freeze on, so I said no. Didn't look right.
Darren: Fair play. I don't think I'd have the willpower, honestly. I'm already browsing what I'm getting next, I'm looking at the new A5. Nicola thinks I'm sad.
Gareth: Each to their own.
Darren: Ha, that's diplomatic. Kids?
Gareth: Two. Josh is sixteen, doing his GCSEs. Ellie's nineteen, she's at uni in Southampton.
Darren: You're joking. My daughter's Ellie, she's sixteen, mocks coming up. And my lad's at uni, Nottingham. It's like looking in a mirror, this. Do you find it quiet with one gone?
Gareth: Er, yeah. Bit. You notice it at dinner, sort of thing. One less plate.
Darren: Yeah, yeah. We've got the dog, Murphy, so he fills the gap. Ate a tea towel last week, an entire tea towel, cost us two hundred quid at the vet. Have you got a dog?
Gareth: Not anymore. Ours died a couple of years ago. Haven't got round to another one.
Darren: Ah, sorry, mate. Anyway, that puzzle at the start, did you finish it? I gave up and guessed half of it.
Gareth: I finished it. Took me a while. The last couple I wasn't sure about.
Darren: You're more patient than me. I'm learn-on-the-job, me, I'm no good with things on paper. That's why I've got an assistant manager who does all my rotas.
Gareth: Rotas I can do. Hundred and eighty staff, we're trialling a new shift pattern at the minute, it's eating my week.
Darren: Hundred and eighty! Blimey. See, you'd want a pint after that. Do you play golf at all?
Gareth: No. I run, mostly. Before work.
Darren: Running. Yeah, I'm more of a nineteenth-hole man, to be honest. I play once a month, badly, and then the bar's the best bit.
Gareth: Sounds about right for most golfers.
Darren: Ha! Exactly. Here, we should get a—

=== CALL C0450 ===
Joanne: Oh. Hello. Sorry, it took a second to connect.
Donna: Hiya. You're alright.
Joanne: Erm, I'm Joanne.
Donna: Donna.
Joanne: Hello.
Donna: So… do we just talk then?
Joanne: I think so. Three minutes, it said.
Donna: Right.
Joanne: Erm, where are you, then?
Donna: Plumstead. South-east London. You?
Joanne: Crawley.
Donna: Oh, near Gatwick.
Joanne: Yeah, right under it, sort of. The planes have been ever so loud lately.
Donna: I bet.
Joanne: Do you, erm… do you do a lot of these? The studies?
Donna: Yeah, a few. Bit of extra money, isn't it. I'm not working at the minute, so.
Joanne: No, me neither, actually. I was made redundant last year. I'd been at the same place seventeen years.
Donna: Seventeen years? That's harsh. What was it?
Joanne: Accounts. At a builders' merchants. They got bought out and moved everything up to Milton Keynes.
Donna: Did they not give you the option?
Joanne: They did, but I wasn't going to move to Milton Keynes. I live with my mum and dad, so.
Donna: Yeah, no, fair enough. I was cleaning, offices in Woolwich, early mornings. Contract ended. I liked it to be fair, nobody about, headphones in, just get on with it.
Joanne: That sounds nice, actually. I'd rather that than the phones.
Donna: Yeah, I can't be doing with phones.
Joanne: No.
Donna: …
Joanne: Erm, did you do the puzzle bit alright?
Donna: Sort of. I got bored halfway through, if I'm honest.
Joanne: I quite liked it. I do word searches and that, so.
Donna: Fair enough.
Joanne: Have you got any pets? I've got a Jack Russell, Bobby. He's quite old now, his back leg's not great.
Donna: No. We're in a flat, it's not really allowed. I've got two kids though, that's enough.
Joanne: How old are they?
Donna: Kyle's sixteen, he's doing his GCSEs this year. And Mia's eleven, she's just started secondary. Lost her blazer already. First month.
Joanne: Oh no.
Donna: Yeah. Forty quid, them blazers. And Kyle's on his PlayStation till all hours, I keep telling him, you've got exams, you was up till two last night. Do you know what I mean? I just want him to sort of get his head down. Do better than I did.
Joanne: Yeah. I'm sure he will.
Donna: Hope so. Have you got kids?
Joanne: No. No, I haven't.
Donna: Right.
Joanne: Erm. Do you watch any of the soaps?
Donna: EastEnders. Every night, pretty much.
Joanne: I'm more Corrie. And Emmerdale. My mum and I watch them after dinner.
Donna: My mum's Corrie. She rings me about it, she rings me about everything, five times a day.
Joanne: Mine's in the next room, so she just shouts.
Donna: Ha. That's worse, to be fair.
Joanne: It is a bit, yeah.

=== CALL C0451 ===
Darren: Hello, hello! Joanne, is it? Can you hear me alright?
Joanne: Yes. Hello. Sorry, my screen froze for a second.
Darren: No worries, you're here now. I'm Darren. Where are you calling from?
Joanne: Crawley.
Darren: Crawley, so right by Gatwick. I'm Basingstoke. What do you do, then?
Joanne: Erm, nothing at the moment. I was in accounts, purchase ledger, at a builders' merchants near Gatwick. Seventeen years. I was made redundant last year.
Darren: You're joking. Builders' merchants? That's me! I'm branch manager at one: yard, trade counter, the lot. Which lot were you with?
Joanne: Erm, I'd rather not say, really. They got bought out anyway, and the back office went up to Milton Keynes.
Darren: Yeah, that's happening all over. Head office loves a centralise. Seventeen years though, that's rough.
Joanne: It was a bit of a shock, yeah.
Darren: I'll tell you what, I could do with someone like you. I'm hopeless on the paperwork side. My assistant manager does all of it: rotas, compliance, stock audits. I leave my reports till the night before, right, and then it's panic stations.
Joanne: Supplier statements were the worst. Reconciling them at month end.
Darren: Oh, don't. We had a rep take me out for a steak lunch the other week, lovely, all very friendly. Then his invoice comes in and the pricing's nothing like what we'd agreed over the steak. So I'm on the phone going, mate, I bought dessert on the strength of that.
Joanne: Erm, that happens a lot. The credit notes never match either.
Darren: Never! They never match. So are you looking for something similar?
Joanne: Sort of. Admin, part-time, something local. Not on the phones, ideally.
Darren: Not phones, yeah, fair enough. My trade counter would eat you alive. Good lads, but they'll shout at you because their copper fittings are late.
Joanne: That's the bit I don't want, really.
Darren: Anyway, yeah. I saw the Jack Russell photo on your wall.
Joanne: Oh. That's Bobby. He's fourteen now. His back leg's playing up, and the vet bills are, erm, a lot.
Darren: Don't talk to me about vets. Murphy, my Lab, ate a whole tea towel last week. Two hundred quid.
Joanne: A whole one?
Darren: The whole thing. And it came out the other end, well, I won't go into that.
Joanne: Bobby ate a sock once.
Darren: They're all the same. Do you walk him much?
Joanne: Tilgate Park, every morning. Same route.
Darren: Lovely. I do Murphy at weekends, mostly. Nicola does the week and she reckons I owe her. Did you do the puzzle bit?
Joanne: Yes. I liked that, actually.
Darren: You'd be the one. I guessed half of mine. And the bloke on my last call finished his and all, so I'm surrounded by clever people today.
Joanne: It was just patterns, really.
Darren: Just patterns, she says. Right, well, if they ever want someone to do the paperwork for this study, I know who I'm—

=== CALL C0452 ===
Gareth: Hello. Can you hear me?
Donna: Yeah. Hiya.
Gareth: I'm Gareth.
Donna: Donna.
Gareth: Right. Er, where are you based?
Donna: Plumstead. South-east London.
Gareth: I'm in Andover. Hampshire.
Donna: Okay.
Gareth: Did you get on alright with the puzzle?
Donna: Not really. I got bored. I just sort of put anything in by the end.
Gareth: Fair enough. I took too long over mine, to be honest.
Donna: Right.
Gareth: What do you do, work-wise?
Donna: Erm, nothing at the minute. I was cleaning offices, early mornings, but the contract ended. So I'm looking. Sort of.
Gareth: Early mornings. I'm the same, I'm in for the six o'clock handover most days. Warehousing. It's the best bit of the day, before everyone starts phoning you.
Donna: Yeah, that's what I liked. Nobody about. Headphones in.
Gareth: We've got cleaners in on the early shift. Good ones are hard to find, honestly. Half the agency people don't turn up.
Donna: Well, I'd turn up. I'm alright once I'm there. It's the admin bit I'm rubbish at. Texts about shifts and that.
Gareth: Sorry, the admin?
Donna: Like, they change your shift by text and I don't see it. Do you know what I mean?
Gareth: Yeah. We've had that. Er, have you got family?
Donna: Two kids. Kyle's sixteen, doing his GCSEs. Mia's eleven.
Gareth: Mine's sixteen as well, Josh. GCSEs. Mocks soon.
Donna: Is he revising?
Gareth: He says he is. His phone's in his hand every time I go in.
Donna: With Kyle it's the PlayStation. Till two in the morning. I keep saying to him, you was the one who said you wanted to do the electrician course, so you need the grades. He just goes "yeah, yeah". I don't want him drifting, you know. I left with nothing much and I don't want that for him.
Gareth: No. Er, with Josh, I'm not home enough to keep on at him, to be honest. My wife does most of it. I'm out early and back late. You sort of miss things.
Donna: At least you're working, though.
Gareth: Yeah. That's true.
Donna: Have you got any others?
Gareth: A daughter, nineteen. She's at uni in Southampton. She comes back most holidays.
Donna: That's not far.
Gareth: No. Close enough. The house is quieter, though.
Donna: Mine's never quiet. My mum's ringing five times a day, Mia's shouting about where her blazer's gone.
Gareth: Do you follow football at all?
Donna: Not really. Charlton, cos my dad did. Kyle has it on.
Gareth: Charlton. Could be worse. I'm Southampton, so I can't say much after Saturday.
Donna: Was it bad?
Gareth: Yeah. Poor.

Donna: Donna.
Gareth: Right. Er, where are you based?
Donna: Plumstead. South-east London.
Gareth: I'm in Andover. Hampshire.
Donna: Okay.
Gareth: Did you get on alright with the puzzle?
Donna: Not really. I got bored. I just sort of put anything in by the end.
Gareth: Fair enough. I took too long over mine, to be honest.
Donna: Right.
Gareth: What do you do, work-wise?
Donna: Erm, nothing at the minute. I was cleaning offices, early mornings, but the contract ended. So I'm looking. Sort of.
Gareth: Early mornings. I'm the same, I'm in for the six o'clock handover most days. Warehousing. It's the best bit of the day, before everyone starts phoning you.
Donna: Yeah, that's what I liked. Nobody about. Headphones in.
Gareth: We've got cleaners in on the early shift. Good ones are hard to find, honestly. Half the agency people don't turn up.
Donna: Well, I'd turn up. I'm alright once I'm there. It's the admin bit I'm rubbish at. Texts about shifts and that.
Gareth: Sorry, the admin?
Donna: Like, they change your shift by text and I don't see it. Do you know what I mean?
Gareth: Yeah. We've had that. Er, have you got family?
Donna: Two kids. Kyle's sixteen, doing his GCSEs. Mia's eleven.
Gareth: Mine's sixteen as well, Josh. GCSEs. Mocks soon.
Donna: Is he revising?
Gareth: He says he is. His phone's in his hand every time I go in.
Donna: With Kyle it's the PlayStation. Till two in the morning. I keep saying to him, you was the one who said you wanted to do the electrician course, so you need the grades. He just goes "yeah, yeah". I don't want him drifting, you know. I left with nothing much and I don't want that for him.
Gareth: No. Er, with Josh, I'm not home enough to keep on at him, to be honest. My wife does most of it. I'm out early and back late. You sort of miss things.
Donna: At least you're working, though.
Gareth: Yeah. That's true.
Donna: Have you got any others?
Gareth: A daughter, nineteen. She's at uni in Southampton. She comes back most holidays.
Donna: That's not far.
Gareth: No. Close enough. The house is quieter, though.
Donna: Mine's never quiet. My mum's ringing five times a day, Mia's shouting about where her blazer's gone.
Gareth: Do you follow football at all?
Donna: Not really. Charlton, cos my dad did. Kyle has it on.
Gareth: Charlton. Could be worse. I'm Southampton, so I can't say much after Saturday.
Donna: Was it bad?
Gareth: Yeah. Poor.
calls.C0453:
Darren: Hello! There she is. Donna, is it? Can you hear me alright?
Donna: Yeah. Hiya.
Darren: I'm Darren. Last one for me, this. Where are you, then?
Donna: Plumstead. South-east London.
Darren: Oh, right, London. I'm Basingstoke. Did you have to come far for this, or is it all on the laptop?
Donna: Sorry, what was that?
Darren: Ha, no, ignore me, obviously it's on the laptop. That was a stupid question. Anyway, yeah. What do you do?
Donna: Nothing at the minute. I was cleaning offices in Woolwich, early mornings. Contract ended.
Darren: Ah, that's a pain. Looking for something?
Donna: Sort of. Cleaning or kitchen porter. Something early so I'm back for my daughter.
Darren: Makes sense. I manage a builders' merchants, yard and trade counter, fourteen staff. Funnily enough the woman I just spoke to used to do accounts at one. Small world today. The bloke before that's a Saints fan from Basingstoke and all, so it's been like a reunion.
Donna: Right.
Darren: How many kids have you got, then?
Donna: Two. Kyle's sixteen, Mia's eleven.
Darren: Sixteen, so GCSEs?
Donna: Yeah. This year.
Darren: My Ellie's the same. Mocks in a couple of weeks. She's alright, to be fair, she's more organised than me. Doesn't take much, mind. How's your lad getting on?
Donna: Erm, he's clever enough, he just doesn't do anything. PlayStation till all hours. He wants to do electrics after, so I keep telling him, you need maths for that, you need English. He thinks I'm nagging. I am nagging, but someone's got to, do you know what I mean? I left school with four GCSEs and I don't want him doing the same.
Darren: Electrician, that's a good shout, though. Proper trade. I tell you what, the sparks that come in my place, they're not short of a few quid. Half of them drive nicer vans than my car, and I've got an Audi.
Donna: Yeah, well. He's got to get on the course first.
Darren: He will. Sixteen-year-old lads are all the same. My son was a nightmare at that age, and now he's at uni in Nottingham, so.
Donna: Is he?
Darren: Yeah. Comes home with his washing. Do you drive at all?
Donna: No.
Darren: No? How do you get about, then?
Donna: Walk, mostly. The buses are rubbish. The 53's always late.
Darren: I'd be lost without the car, me. I sat on the M3 forty minutes on Tuesday, mind, so maybe you've got the right idea.
Donna: I'm not paying for a car anyway. The electric's gone up enough.
Darren: Oh, it's criminal, the bills. Anyway, yeah. What do you do on a Friday? Takeaway sort of person?
Donna: Chinese, if there's money.
Darren: Curry for us. Every Friday, without fail. The dog sits there looking at you like he's never been fed.
Donna: You've got a dog, haven't you? I saw it on your picture.
Darren: Murphy. Black Lab. Ate a tea towel last week. Whole thing.
Donna: Ha. Mia would love a dog. Not allowed in the flat, though.
Darren: Probably for the best. Two hundred quid at the vet, that tea towel. More than the—
calls.C0454:
Gareth: Hello. Can you hear me okay?
Joanne: Erm, yes. Hello. Sorry, I was just checking my sound.
Gareth: No problem. I'm Gareth.
Joanne: Joanne.
Gareth: Where are you?
Joanne: Crawley.
Gareth: Andover, me.
Joanne: Right.
Gareth: Er, did you do alright with the puzzle?
Joanne: I think so. I quite liked it.
Gareth: Same. Took me a while, though.
Joanne: Yeah.
Gareth: What do you do, work-wise?
Joanne: Erm, I'm between jobs. I was purchase ledger for seventeen years at a builders' merchants. Made redundant when they got bought out.
Gareth: Seventeen years. That's a long time to give somewhere.
Joanne: It was, yeah. The man I spoke to before runs one, actually. A builders' merchants.
Gareth: Darren? Basingstoke? I had him first.
Joanne: Yes. He's, erm, quite chatty.
Gareth: He is, yeah. Nice enough bloke. I'm in warehousing, operations. We've got three sites. Honestly, people like you are the ones I'd keep if I had the choice. Everyone thinks it's the forklift drivers who keep the place running, and they do, but if purchase ledger's a mess you find out three months later when a haulier's charging you twice for the same load and nobody's noticed. Good accounts people catch that.
Joanne: Erm, that used to happen. Duplicate invoices. I'd always check against the delivery notes.
Gareth: That's exactly it. Are you looking for the same sort of thing?
Joanne: Part-time, ideally. Somewhere local. Not on reception or phones.
Gareth: Makes sense. Agencies always want to stick people on reception.
Joanne: They do. I've turned a couple down.
Gareth: Fair enough.
Joanne: Erm.
Gareth: I saw you've got a dog. In the photo.
Joanne: Oh. Bobby. Jack Russell. He's fourteen.
Gareth: We had a spaniel. She died a couple of years back. Haven't had the heart for another yet.
Joanne: Oh, I'm sorry. Bobby's back leg's going, so I do sort of think about it.
Gareth: Yeah. You don't think about it till it happens. Do you walk him much?
Joanne: Every morning. Tilgate Park. Same way round each time.
Gareth: I'm the same with running. Same route every day, about five k. My wife says I'd get lost if they moved a tree.
Joanne: My mum says that about me.
Gareth: Do you get away at all? Holidays?
Joanne: Isle of Wight. Caravan, every September, with my mum and dad.
Gareth: We do the Algarve. Same place, eight years running. I can't be doing with looking for somewhere new.
Joanne: No. I don't like flying, so.
Gareth: Airports are a hassle anyway. The A303's bad enough in August.
Joanne: Is it the—

C0452.line_text: No. Close enough. The house is quieter, though.
C0452.what: Before speaking, Gareth looks away to his left towards the window for about three seconds with his lips pressed together, then looks back at the screen.
